proof_strategy_taxonomy.description: Partition problem into exhaustive cases based on variable constraints or function behavior. Dominant in algebra (379/834=45.4% of Level 4-5) where piecewise functions and multi-condition constraints require systematic enumeration. Essential for geometry (598/870=68.7% hard) where configuration cases depend on relative point positions.

Introduce new variables to simplify complex expressions, symmetrize equations, or reveal hidden structure. Found in 360/834=43.2% of hard algebra solutions where rationalizing substitutions or symmetry-breaking variables transform intractable equations.

Draw additional geometric elements to reveal hidden structure. Observed in 431/598=72.1% of hard geometry solutions where strategic auxiliary lines (perpendiculars, angle bisectors, circles through key points) expose similarity or cyclic quadrilateral properties invisible in original configuration.

Apply sequential trigonometric identities to transform complex angle relations. Found in 433/598=72.4% of hard geometry and 256/352=72.7% of hard precalculus solutions, using angle addition formulas, product-to-sum identities, and inverse relations in multi-step derivations.

Decompose integers into prime powers and analyze exponent parity or modular constraints. Dominant in number theory (261/500=52.2% of Level 4-5) where perfect square conditions, divisibility chains, and Diophantine feasibility depend on prime exponent structures.

Build successive congruence relations modulo strategically chosen bases. Found in 168/500=33.6% of hard number theory solutions, using Chinese Remainder Theorem connections or lifting exponent lemma to constrain solution sets through residue analysis.

Map discrete counting or probability questions to continuous geometric regions, computing ratios of areas/volumes. Characteristic of hard counting problems (observed in Level 5 solutions at 276/771=35.8% frequency) where uniform distribution assumptions translate to measure-theoretic calculations.

Define recurrence relations over system states for sequential decision problems. Found in complex counting problems requiring dynamic programming approaches, where state transitions encode combinatorial constraints across multiple steps.

Use matrix representations of linear transformations to find invariant subspaces, eigenvalues, or projection formulas. Found in 103/352=29.3% of hard precalculus solutions where reflection, rotation, and projection matrices encode geometric operations algebraically.

Project vectors onto optimal subspaces using dot product structure. Observed in 106/352=30.1% of hard precalculus solutions where minimizing distances or finding closest points reduces to orthogonal projection calculations.

reasoning_style_comparison.algebra: Algebra exhibits 834/1744=47.8% hard-problem concentration with solutions averaging 1.9x length increase from Level 3 to Level 5. Dominant pattern: case analysis (45.4% of hard solutions) driven by piecewise functions and multi-constraint systems. First-step characteristic: variable substitution or system setup. Structural shift: from direct evaluation (Level 3) to nested case branching with verification requirements (Level 5).
reasoning_style_comparison.geometry: Geometry shows highest hard-problem rate at 598/870=68.7% with steepest difficulty gradient. Solutions expand 1.9x in length from Level 3 to Level 5. Dominant patterns: auxiliary construction (72.1%) and trigonometric chains (72.4%) requiring spatial reasoning. First-step characteristic: strategic coordinate placement or auxiliary element drawing. Solutions fail when auxiliary construction existence assumptions violate implicit non-degeneracy constraints.
reasoning_style_comparison.counting_and_probability: Counting & Probability has 442/771=57.3% hard rate with largest length expansion (2.1x Level 3 to Level 5). Dominant patterns: casework analysis (31.0%) and bijection arguments. First-step characteristic: state space definition or complementary set identification. Unique structural feature: continuous geometric probability mapping requiring measure-theoretic intuition distinct from discrete enumeration.
reasoning_style_comparison.number_theory: Number Theory shows 500/869=57.5% hard-problem concentration with systematic solution structure. Dominant patterns: prime factorization (52.2%) and modular arithmetic (33.6%). First-step characteristic: residue class reduction or prime power decomposition. Solutions require careful verification against small cases where patterns may fail, evidenced by 19.6% of hard solutions including explicit check statements.
reasoning_style_comparison.precalculus: Precalculus has lowest hard-problem rate at 352/746=47.2% but longest absolute solution length (Level 5 average 1359 chars). Dominant patterns: trigonometric identities (72.7%), vector analysis (30.1%), and matrix methods (29.3%). First-step characteristic: parameterization or coordinate system selection. High prevalence (38.4%) of branch selection indicators reflects multi-valued function complexity requiring explicit choice of principal values.

most_subtle_reasoning_failure_modes: Geometry Missing Auxiliary Construction Verification (598/870=68.7% Level 4-5): Solutions that skip verifying auxiliary construction existence fail in the congruence step when assumed intersection points lie outside valid geometric constraints. Only 3.7% of hard geometry solutions include explicit WLOG or general position statements, leaving unstated assumptions that cause reasoning collapse.

Number Theory Incomplete Modular Case Coverage (500/869=57.5% hard): Solutions missing residue class analysis fail at periodic boundary conditions, particularly when small cases violate general patterns derived from modular arguments. 19.6% of hard number theory solutions include explicit verification statements, indicating widespread need for case-checking that many solutions omit.

Algebra Extraneous Solution Introduction (834/1744=47.8% hard): Solutions without domain constraint verification introduce extraneous roots from squared equations or radical extractions. Only 6.8% of hard algebra solutions explicitly check domain validity despite prevalence of substitution strategies that can expand solution sets non-equivalently.

Counting & Probability Symmetry Overcounting (442/771=57.3% hard): Solutions failing to account for rotational symmetry overcount distinct configurations by failing to divide by symmetry order. Overcounting corrections appear in only 9.5% of hard C&P solutions despite being essential for problems with identical elements or symmetric arrangements.

Precalculus Incorrect Branch Selection (352/746=47.2% hard): Solutions without explicit branch selection yield incorrect arguments for complex roots and inverse trigonometric functions. Branch selection indicators appear in 38.4% of hard precalculus solutions, reflecting the prevalence of multi-valued reasoning failures where principal values are implicitly assumed without justification.

cross_domain_reasoning_transfer: Domains rank by hard-problem rate: (1) geometry 598/870=68.7%, (2) number_theory 500/869=57.5%, (3) counting_and_probability 442/771=57.3%, (4) algebra 834/1744=47.8%, (5) precalculus 352/746=47.2%. Geometry's highest rate reflects auxiliary construction creativity requirement. Number theory and counting share similar hard rates (~57%) but differ structurally: number theory uses systematic modular chains while counting requires state space abstraction. Algebra and precalculus share lowest rates (~47%) but differ in precalculus having longer solutions requiring explicit branch selection. Solution-text patterns transfer across domains: trigonometric transformations bridge geometry (72.4% of hard) and precalculus (72.7% of hard); case analysis spans algebra (45.4%), counting (31.0%), and number theory (indirectly through modular cases). Auxiliary construction in geometry (72.1%) transfers to vector projection in precalculus (30.1%) as geometric intuition applied algebraically. Failure modes show domain-specificity: geometry fails on unstated auxiliary assumptions, number theory on incomplete modular coverage, algebra on extraneous solutions, counting on symmetry overcounting, precalculus on branch selection.
